replacement: Alyosha had not been there for four days, and he was in a hurry to go straight up to Lise, because she was the one he needed to talk to. Lise had sent a maid to him the day before with a special request that he come and see her “about something very important,” and for certain reasons that request interested Alyosha. But while the maid was gone to announce him to Lise, Madame Hohlakov heard from someone that he had arrived and at once sent a message begging him to come to her “for just one minute.” Alyosha decided it was best to give in to the mamma’s request, or else she would keep sending down to Lise’s room every minute he was there. Madame Hohlakov was lying on her couch. She was dressed with particular elegance and was obviously in a state of extreme nervous excitement. She greeted Alyosha with cries of rapture.

“I can sit up. Oh, you’ve muddled me! Oh, this trial, this savage deed, and then they’re all off to Siberia, some are getting married, and all of it so fast, so fast, everything changing, and in the end—nothing. Everybody grows old with death ahead of them. Well, so be it! I’m weary. This Katya, _cette charmante personne_, has let down all my hopes. Now she’s going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother is going to follow her and settle in the nearest town, and they’ll all torment one another. It drives me out of my mind. Worst of all is the publicity. The story has been told a million times in all the papers in Moscow and Petersburg. Oh, and would you believe it, one of them says I was ‘a dear friend’ of your brother’s ——, I can’t bring myself to say the horrid word. Just imagine, just imagine!”

“Well, then, I’ll tell you everything. It can’t be helped, I’ll make a confession, since there is one point where I may have been at fault. Only a tiny, tiny point, so tiny that perhaps it doesn’t count. You see, my dear boy”—Madame Hohlakov suddenly turned arch, and a charming, enigmatic smile played on her lips—“you see, I suspect ... You must forgive me, Alyosha. I’m like a mother to you.... No, no, just the opposite. I’m speaking to you now as if you were my father—mother is quite out of place. Well, it’s as though I were confessing to Father Zossima, that’s exactly it. I called you a monk just now. So then, that poor young man, your friend Rakitin (Mercy on us! I can’t be angry with him. I’m cross, but not very), that frivolous young man, would you believe it, seems to have got it into his head that he’s in love with me. I only noticed later. At first, a month ago, he merely began coming to see me more often, nearly every day, though of course we knew each other before. I suspected nothing ... and then all at once it dawned on me, and I started noticing things, with astonishment. You know, two months ago that modest, charming, excellent young man, Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who’s in the service here, became a regular visitor. You’ve met him here ever so many times yourself. And he’s such an excellent, serious young man, isn’t he? He comes once every three days, not daily (though I’d be glad to see him daily), and always so well dressed. In short, I love young people, Alyosha, talented and modest ones, like you. And he has nearly a statesman’s mind, he talks so charmingly, and I’ll certainly, certainly try to get him promoted. He’s a diplomat in the making. On that awful day he almost saved me from death by coming in the night. And your friend Rakitin turns up in such boots, and always stretches them out on the carpet.... Then he began to hint at his feelings, and one day as he was leaving he squeezed my hand terribly hard. My foot began to swell right after he’d pressed my hand like that. He’d met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe it, he’s forever sneering at him, snarling at him, for no reason I can see. I simply watched the two of them together and laughed to myself. So I was sitting here alone—no, I was laid up then. Well, I was lying here alone when suddenly in comes Rakitin, and just imagine! He’d brought me some verses of his own writing—a little poem about my bad foot, that is, he’d described my foot in a poem. Wait a moment—how did it go?

“I’ll tell you. This Katya ... Ah! She’s a charming, charming creature, but I can never make out who she’s in love with. She was here a while back and I couldn’t get a word out of her. All the more because now she only chats with me about trifles. It’s my health, my health, nothing else, and what a tone she takes with me! So I just said to myself, ‘Well, so be it. I don’t care’... Oh, yes. I was talking about aberration. The doctor has arrived. You know a doctor has arrived? Of course you do—the one who finds out who is mad. You sent for him. No, not you, it was Katya. It’s all Katya’s doing. Now, you see, a man can sit there perfectly sane and all at once have an aberration. He may be fully aware and know what he’s doing, and still be in a state of aberration. And there’s no doubt that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. People found out about aberration the moment the law courts were reformed. It’s all the fine result of the reformed courts. The doctor was here and asked me about that evening, about the gold mines. ‘How did he seem then?’ he asked. He must have been in a state of aberration. He burst in shouting, ‘Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!’ and then he left and did the murder straight away. ‘I don’t want to murder him,’ he said, and suddenly he went and murdered him. That is why they will acquit him: he fought against it, and yet he murdered him.”

“From aberration. When he came round from the blow Dmitri Fyodorovitch gave him on the head, he was in a state of aberration, and he went and did the murder. As for his saying he didn’t, very likely he just doesn’t remember. Only, you know, it would be better, ever so much better, if it was Dmitri Fyodorovitch who murdered him. And that’s how it must have been, though I keep saying Grigory. It was certainly Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that’s better, ever so much better! Oh! I don’t mean it’s better that a son should kill his father. I don’t defend that. Children should honor their parents. And yet it would be better if it were he, because then you’d have nothing to weep over, since he did it unconscious—or rather conscious, but without knowing what he was doing. Let them acquit him! That is so humane, and it would show what a blessing the reformed courts are. I knew nothing about all this, but they say the courts have been reformed for a long time. When I heard of it yesterday I was so struck that I wanted to send for you at once. And if he’s acquitted, make him come straight from the courtroom to dine with me. I’ll invite a party of friends and we’ll drink to the reformed courts. I don’t think he’d be dangerous. Besides, I’ll ask a great many friends, so that he could always be led out if he tried anything. And afterwards he could be made a justice of the peace or something in another town, since those who have been in trouble themselves make the best judges. And anyway, who isn’t suffering from aberration these days?—you, I, all of us are in a state of aberration, and there are plenty of examples. A man sits singing a song, something suddenly annoys him, he picks up a pistol and shoots the first person he sees, and nobody blames him. I read that recently, and all the doctors confirm it. The doctors are forever confirming; they’ll confirm anything. Why, my Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday, and the day before, and today I suddenly saw that it’s all aberration. Oh, Lise grieves me so! I think she is completely mad. Why did she send for you? Did she send for you, or did you come of your own accord?”
“Oh, yes. You won’t forget, you won’t forget what I asked you, will you? It’s a matter of life and death!”
